question: During a Kubernetes rolling upgrade, what happens to active rooms on the pod being replaced?
options: All rooms are seamlessly migrated to another node with no interruption
The upgrade waits indefinitely until all rooms on that pod are empty
Participants receive a disconnect event and the client SDK automatically reconnects to a healthy node, typically within 1-3 seconds
Active rooms are permanently lost and participants must manually rejoin
explanation: When a pod is replaced, its connections drain. Participants receive a disconnect event and the LiveKit client SDK handles reconnection automatically. The long terminationGracePeriodSeconds gives rooms time to finish naturally, but if they are still active when the grace period expires, the disconnect-and-reconnect flow kicks in.

question: Why should you NOT back up LiveKit media streams as part of your disaster recovery plan?
options: Media files are too large to store cost-effectively
Media encryption prevents backup tools from reading the data
Media streams are real-time and ephemeral -- they cannot be serialized, stored, or restored. Backup protects infrastructure and configuration, not individual call sessions
LiveKit automatically backs up media to Redis
explanation: Active voice and video calls are real-time bidirectional streams over WebRTC. They cannot be paused, serialized, and resumed from a backup. When LiveKit restarts, participants reconnect and rejoin. Backup protects your ability to resume service, not to preserve individual sessions.

question: What is the recommended approach before performing a major version upgrade of LiveKit?
options: Back up Redis, test the upgrade in staging, read the changelog for breaking changes, then schedule a maintenance window for production
Immediately upgrade production to minimize the time spent on an old version
Stop all active rooms first, then upgrade all nodes simultaneously
Roll back to the oldest supported version first, then upgrade to the latest
explanation: Major versions may include Redis schema migrations and breaking config changes. Backing up Redis protects against rollback incompatibility. Testing in staging catches issues before they affect users. Reading the changelog identifies any manual migration steps. A maintenance window ensures all nodes upgrade together when the protocol requires it.
